title: Boundedness Of The Hardy-Littlewood Maximal Operator On Generalized Fofana Spaces
authors: Pokou Nagacy, Berenger Akon Kpata, Nouffou Diarra
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce generalized Fofana spaces and we give some of their basic properties. These spaces are a kind of generalization of generalized Morrey spaces. As application, we establish the boundedness of the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator on these new spaces.
tldr: The paper introduces generalized Fofana spaces and proves boundedness of the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator on them.
motivation: To extend the theory of function spaces, specifically generalizing Morrey spaces, and to study operator boundedness in these new spaces.
method: Definition of generalized Fofana spaces and functional analysis techniques to prove boundedness of the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator.
result: The Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator is bounded on the newly defined generalized Fofana spaces.
conclusion: The work contributes to harmonic analysis and function space theory, with potential applications in partial differential equations and analysis.

title: Runge--Kutta Numerical Methods For Ruin Probabilities In Classical Risk Model
authors: Lazaros Kanellopoulos George Kanakoudis
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study Runge--Kutta methods for the computation of ruin probabilities in the classical risk model through the associated Volterra integro-differential equation. The proposed framework combines fourth-order one-step and two-step Runge--Kutta schemes with numerical quadrature formulas to approximate the convolution term. In particular, the convolution term is approximated using Newton--Cotes and Gaussian quadrature formulas, including Simpson's 1/3 rule and Pareto-adapted Gauss--Jacobi quadrature. An equivalent reformulation of the Volterra equation as a system of ordinary differential equations is also considered. Implementations for Gamma and Pareto claim-size distributions are developed. Numerical results are presented to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
tldr: This paper applies Runge-Kutta numerical methods to compute ruin probabilities in classical risk models, which is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, or condensed matter physics.
motivation: Ruin probability computation is important in actuarial science and risk management, but this work does not connect to quantum or information-theoretic topics.
method: The authors use fourth-order one-step and two-step Runge-Kutta schemes combined with Newton-Cotes and Gaussian quadrature to solve the Volterra integro-differential equation for ruin probabilities.
result: Numerical experiments for Gamma and Pareto claim-size distributions demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
conclusion: The methods provide accurate and efficient computation of ruin probabilities, but the paper has no relevance to quantum computing, information thermodynamics, or related fields.

title: Hybrid And Component-wise Leggett-Williams Type Fixed Point Theorems In Product Spaces With Applications
authors: Laura Mar\'ia Fern\'andez-Pardo
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we present new multiplicity fixed point theorems for operators acting on Cartesian products of two normed linear spaces. We show that Leggett-Williams type conditions in each component of the system guarantee the existence of nine distinct fixed points, of which four of them are coexistence fixed points, i.e., points with all components nontrivial. In addition, a hybrid approach combining Leggett-Williams conditions in one component with Krasnosel'skii compression-expansion conditions in the other allows us to obtain three fixed points. As an application, we establish the existence of multiple positive solutions for nonlinear systems of second-order equations with two-point boundary conditions.
tldr: This paper proves new fixed point theorems of Leggett-Williams type in product spaces and applies them to systems of second-order boundary value problems.
motivation: To extend fixed point theory to product spaces and obtain multiple coexistence fixed points for nonlinear systems.
method: Uses component-wise Leggett-Williams conditions and a hybrid approach combining Leggett-Williams with Krasnosel'skii compression-expansion conditions.
result: Establishes existence of nine distinct fixed points (four coexistence) under component-wise conditions, and three fixed points under hybrid conditions.
conclusion: Provides new tools for proving existence of multiple positive solutions to nonlinear boundary value problems, with potential applications in differential equations.

title: Ergodicity Of $c^2$ Minimal Actions Of Thompson Group $t$ On The Circle
authors: Klaudiusz Czudek
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that every [MATH] minimal action of Thompson group [MATH] on the circle is ergodic with respect to the Lebesgue measure. If such action is not minimal then the Lebesgue measure of the exceptional minimal set is zero.
tldr: This paper proves ergodicity of certain minimal actions of Thompson group T on the circle with respect to Lebesgue measure.
motivation: To understand ergodic properties of group actions on the circle, specifically for Thompson group T, which is a finitely presented group with interesting dynamical properties.
method: The paper uses dynamical systems and ergodic theory techniques, likely involving analysis of minimal sets and invariant measures.
result: Every C^2 minimal action of Thompson group T on the circle is ergodic with respect to Lebesgue measure; if not minimal, the exceptional minimal set has Lebesgue measure zero.
conclusion: The results contribute to the classification of actions of Thompson group T and may have implications for the study of group actions on the circle.

title: Quasi-optimal Polytopal Finite Element Methods For Biharmonic Equation
authors: Ngoc Tien Tran
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper establishes quasi-optimal and lower-order error estimates for weak Galerkin, discontinuous Galerkin, and hybrid-high order finite element methods for the biharmonic equation under minimal regularity assumptions on general polytopal meshes. Furthermore, it is shown that the stabilization is an efficient contribution in a~posteriori error estimators.
tldr: This paper develops quasi-optimal error estimates for polytopal finite element methods applied to the biharmonic equation.
motivation: To establish rigorous error bounds for weak Galerkin, discontinuous Galerkin, and hybrid-high order methods on general polytopal meshes under minimal regularity.
method: Theoretical analysis using finite element techniques to derive a priori and a posteriori error estimates.
result: Quasi-optimal and lower-order error estimates are proven, and stabilization is shown to be efficient in a posteriori error estimators.
conclusion: The results provide a theoretical foundation for these methods on polytopal meshes, with implications for computational mechanics.

title: Billiard Lawn Mowers
authors: Sangsan Warakkagun Natnaree Sriprasert
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the Lawn Mowing Problem restricted to periodic billiard paths in the unit square. Given the combinatorial data of a trajectory, we determine the optimal covering radius, and identify the shortest path that covers the square for any fixed blade radius.
tldr: This paper studies the Lawn Mowing Problem for periodic billiard paths in a unit square, determining optimal covering radii and shortest paths for a given blade radius.
motivation: The Lawn Mowing Problem is a classic geometric optimization problem; this work extends it to periodic billiard trajectories, which have applications in robotics and coverage path planning.
method: The authors analyze combinatorial data of billiard trajectories in the unit square and derive optimal covering radii and shortest paths using geometric and combinatorial reasoning.
result: They determine the optimal covering radius for any given combinatorial trajectory and identify the shortest path that covers the square for a fixed blade radius.
conclusion: The results provide a complete solution for the Lawn Mowing Problem on periodic billiard paths, with potential extensions to other domains or more complex geometries.

title: Refined Convergence Structures Of The Rectangular Raviart-Thomas Element
authors: Yifan Yue, Hongtao Chen, Shuo Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we fully explore three refined convergence structures of the lowest-order rectangular Raviart-Thomas element in solving the Laplace eigenvalue problem. Firstly, the scheme possesses a property of supercloseness between the discrete eigenfunctions and the interpolated ones, so that post-processing can be easily constructed to improve the accuracy at most by one order. The essentially skillful method is the integral expansion for interpolation terms. Secondly, based on the supercloseness property, we derive the error expansions for not only simple eigenvalues but also multiple eigenvalues, and provide a rigorous proof for them, based on which Richardson extrapolation can be performed. As a byproduct, we prove that all eigenvalues converge from above. Moreover, by utilizing the supercloseness property and Rayleigh quotient analysis, we give a rigorous proof for the convergence behavior for multiple eigenvalues on uniform meshes for the problem on the square domain. Thirdly, the equivalence between the lowest-order rectangular Raviart-Thomas element and the enriched rotated bilinear element is also indicated. At the last of this work, several numerical experiments are designed to demonstrate our theory.
tldr: This paper analyzes convergence properties of the rectangular Raviart-Thomas finite element for Laplace eigenvalue problems, focusing on supercloseness and error expansions.
motivation: To improve accuracy and understanding of eigenvalue approximations using low-order finite elements.
method: Integral expansion for interpolation terms, Richardson extrapolation, and Rayleigh quotient analysis.
result: Supercloseness property enables post-processing to improve accuracy; error expansions for simple and multiple eigenvalues are derived; eigenvalues converge from above.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous convergence analysis and suggests practical improvements for eigenvalue computations.

title: Stability Analysis Of Pantograph Delay Differential Equations
authors: Sachin Bhalekar
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article investigates the stability of pantograph delay differential equations, in which the delayed argument is proportional to the present time. We derive analytic criteria that partition the parameter plane into unstable, asymptotically stable, and delay-dependent stability regions. The theoretical results are supported by numerical simulations that illustrate the sharpness of the stability boundaries. We also formulate a proportional-delay analogue of the Mackey--Glass chaotic delay differential equation and examine the resulting dynamical behaviour.
tldr: This paper studies stability of pantograph delay differential equations, which are unrelated to the user's research interests.
motivation: To understand stability properties of delay differential equations with proportional delay, which appear in certain applied mathematics contexts.
method: Analytical derivation of stability criteria in parameter space, supported by numerical simulations.
result: Identified regions of instability, asymptotic stability, and delay-dependent stability; also formulated a proportional-delay Mackey-Glass chaotic equation.
conclusion: Provides theoretical stability boundaries and demonstrates chaotic behavior in a new delay system, but has no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Life Without "Choice"
authors: M. A. Sofi
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an AC-independent proof of the existence of a non-measurable set as a consequence of the Hahn-Banach theorem of functional analysis which is known to be strictly weaker than AC.
tldr: The paper proves the existence of a non-measurable set using the Hahn-Banach theorem, without relying on the Axiom of Choice.
motivation: To investigate the logical strength of the Hahn-Banach theorem in producing non-measurable sets, independent of the Axiom of Choice.
method: The author provides a proof that the Hahn-Banach theorem implies the existence of a non-measurable set, using functional analysis techniques.
result: A non-measurable set exists as a consequence of the Hahn-Banach theorem, which is strictly weaker than the Axiom of Choice.
conclusion: The result contributes to foundational mathematics, but has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, or condensed matter physics.

title: Achieving Directional-Stationarity From A Single Random Direction Step
authors: Nadav Hallak Dan Greenstein
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of obtaining strong optimality guarantees in constrained nonsmooth nonconvex optimization under mild regularity conditions, namely local Lipschitz continuity and existence and continuity of directional derivatives. While standard methods typically ensure weak stationarity notions, achieving directional (d-)stationarity remains nontrivial. We show that a random direction exploration step is sufficient to attain d-stationarity. The proposed approach augments any base optimization method with a single exploration step that samples a direction and step size and accepts the candidate based on a function value comparison. The resulting scheme guarantees that all accumulation points are d-stationary almost surely, independently of the behavior of the underlying method. Moreover, it preserves convergence rates of the base method, as established for DCA and prox-linear-type schemes. The theoretical results are complemented by numerical experiments illustrating the effect and guarantees of the exploration step.
tldr: This paper proposes a random direction exploration step to achieve directional stationarity in constrained nonsmooth nonconvex optimization.
motivation: Standard optimization methods often only guarantee weak stationarity; achieving directional stationarity under mild regularity conditions is challenging.
method: The approach augments any base optimization method with a single random direction exploration step that samples a direction and step size, accepting the candidate based on function value comparison.
result: All accumulation points are d-stationary almost surely, independent of the base method, and convergence rates of the base method are preserved.
conclusion: The exploration step provides strong optimality guarantees for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization with minimal overhead.

title: Spectra Of Generators Of Hyperbolic Composition And Weighted Composition Semigroups
authors: Ze-Hua Zhou Yong-Xin Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we provide complete characterizations for the spectrum, essential spectrum, and point spectrum of the generators of weighted composition [MATH]-semigroups induced by hyperbolic semiflows on Bergman spaces. We give an explicit example showing that the spectral properties can be influenced by the behavior of the semigroup near non-fixed self-contact points.
tldr: This paper characterizes spectra of generators of weighted composition semigroups on Bergman spaces induced by hyperbolic semiflows.
motivation: To understand spectral properties of generators of composition semigroups, which are important in operator theory and dynamical systems.
method: Functional analysis and operator theory techniques, including spectral theory of semigroups and composition operators.
result: Complete characterizations of the spectrum, essential spectrum, and point spectrum are provided, with an example showing influence of behavior near non-fixed self-contact points.
conclusion: The results advance the theory of composition semigroups, but the paper is purely mathematical with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Simple Derivation Of The Fourier Transform Of The Heaviside Function
authors: Robert C. Dalang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a rigorous derivation of the Fourier transform of the Heaviside function within a framework for tempered distributions that is suitable for undergraduate engineering and mathematics students. The proofs rely on fundamental concepts typically taught in a freshman-level calculus course, including limits, generalized integrals, integration by parts and the Taylor Remainder Theorem.
tldr: This paper provides a rigorous derivation of the Fourier transform of the Heaviside function using elementary calculus, aimed at undergraduate students.
motivation: To offer a simple, accessible derivation of a standard result in distribution theory that avoids advanced functional analysis.
method: Uses limits, generalized integrals, integration by parts, and the Taylor remainder theorem within the framework of tempered distributions.
result: A clear, step-by-step derivation of the Fourier transform of the Heaviside function is presented.
conclusion: The paper serves as a pedagogical tool; no new research contributions or implications for the user's interests.

title: Frequency-Domain Regularized Adversarial Alignment For Transferable Attacks Against Closed-Source MLLMs
authors: Leitao Yuan, Qinghua Mao, Daizong Liu, Kun Wang, Wenjie Wang, Yan Teng, Jing Shao, Dongrui Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remain vulnerable to transfer-based targeted attacks, where perturbations optimized on open-source surrogate encoders can generalize to closed-source MLLMs. A key challenge for improving adversarial transferability is to effectively capture the intrinsic visual focus shared across different models, such that perturbations align with transferable semantic cues rather than surrogate-specific behaviors. However, existing methods suffer from spatial-domain feature redundancy and surrogate-specific gradient signals, thereby hindering cross-model transferability. In this paper, we propose FRA-Attack, which addresses both challenges from a unified frequency-domain regularization perspective. For feature alignment, a high-pass DCT objective on patch features suppresses redundant global structures and concentrates the loss on the high-frequency band that carries the MLLMs' intrinsic visual focus. For gradient optimization, we introduce Frequency-domain Gradient Regularization (FGR), a low-pass regularizer that modulates the surrogate gradient using only the geometric frequency coordinate, , no surrogate-derived statistic is involved, so that FGR is model-agnostic by construction, removing surrogate-specific high-frequency artifacts while preserving transferable low-frequency directions. Together, the two components form a unified frequency-domain treatment of transferability. Extensive experiments on [MATH] flagship MLLMs across [MATH] vendors show that FRA-Attack achieves superior cross-model transferability, particularly with state-of-the-art performance on GPT-5.4, Claude-Opus-4.6 and Gemini-3-flash.
tldr: This paper proposes a frequency-domain regularization method to improve transferable adversarial attacks against closed-source multimodal large language models.
motivation: Existing transfer-based targeted attacks suffer from spatial-domain feature redundancy and surrogate-specific gradient signals, limiting cross-model transferability.
method: FRA-Attack uses a high-pass DCT objective on patch features for feature alignment and a low-pass Frequency-domain Gradient Regularization (FGR) that is model-agnostic to remove surrogate-specific artifacts.
result: Extensive experiments on multiple flagship MLLMs show superior cross-model transferability, with state-of-the-art performance on GPT-5.4, Claude-Opus-4.6, and Gemini-3-flash.
conclusion: The frequency-domain approach effectively enhances adversarial transferability, but the paper focuses on adversarial attacks, which is not aligned with the user's research interests.

title: Assemblage-deephistory: A Cross-Build Binary Dataset With Temporal Coverage
authors: Chang Liu, Noah Fleischmann, Nicol\`o Altamura, Edward Raff, James Holt, Kristopher Micinski
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing binary corpora typically capture only one or two axes of binary variation: they either provide cross-compiler builds without a temporal axis, or CVE labels for single-build binaries. None combine cross-build diversity, cross-version history, and CVE labels into a queryable structure. We present ASSEMBLAGE-DEEPHISTORY, which consolidates these dimensions into a unified framework where every binary's compilation context, source code, vulnerable functions, and package version are stored as first-class metadata. ASSEMBLAGE-DEEPHISTORY comprises 73,610 binaries spanning 248 open-source projects, compiled across GCC, Clang, and MSVC at multiple optimization levels on Linux and Windows, with multi-year historical builds. Each binary is indexed in a database that links it to its source code, functions, debug info, variant builds, historical versions, and vulnerable functions. Three analyses demonstrate this structure's value: (1) a three-stage LLM benchmark (recognition, strategy-guided detection, and cross-build transfer) to test whether LLMs reason about binary vulnerabilities or pattern-match on build-specific artifacts; (2) a comparison of MalConv embeddings, jTrans function embeddings, and TLSH fuzzy hashes quantifying how same-package versions cluster in each space; and (3) a Bayesian regression decomposing binary similarity into contributions from temporal distance, file changes, and commits.
tldr: This paper introduces a large-scale binary dataset with cross-build, temporal, and CVE metadata, and demonstrates its use for LLM vulnerability analysis and binary similarity.
motivation: Existing binary corpora lack combined cross-build diversity, version history, and vulnerability labels, hindering research on binary analysis and security.
method: The authors compiled 73,610 binaries from 248 open-source projects across multiple compilers, optimization levels, and historical versions, and indexed them with source code, functions, and CVE labels. They performed three analyses: LLM benchmark, embedding comparison, and Bayesian regression.
result: The dataset enables studying LLM reasoning vs. pattern-matching, clustering of same-package versions in embedding spaces, and decomposition of binary similarity into temporal and code-change factors.
conclusion: Assemblage-deephistory provides a valuable resource for binary analysis research, but is not directly relevant to the user's interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, or foundations.

title: Adversarial Reframing: A Framework For Targeted Generation In Language Models
authors: Shahnewaz Karim Sakib, Swati Kar, Anindya Bijoy Das
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely deployed in diverse real-world settings, yet remain vulnerable to jailbreaking, where prompt-based attacks bypass safety filters. We present THREAT (Targeted Harmful generation via Reframing and Exploitation of Adversarial Tactics), a reasoning-driven framework that coordinates multiple LLMs in an iterative search loop to find textual jailbreak prompts. We formulate prompt discovery as a nonconvex optimization problem and provide an efficient solution that lowers runtime and improves attack effectiveness. Across diverse datasets and model architectures, THREAT delivers higher attack success rates with lower computational cost than prior methods. The crafted prompts were flagged as harmful in fewer than 1% of cases, compared with about 50% refusals for the corresponding unmodified prompts. These findings reveal previously undetected vulnerabilities in aligned LLMs and position THREAT as a practical tool for proactively strengthening the safety of foundation models.
tldr: This paper presents a framework for generating adversarial jailbreak prompts against LLMs, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The research aims to expose vulnerabilities in LLMs by developing efficient methods to generate harmful prompts that bypass safety filters.
method: The authors propose THREAT, a multi-LLM iterative search framework that formulates prompt discovery as a nonconvex optimization problem.
result: THREAT achieves higher attack success rates with lower computational cost than prior methods, and crafted prompts are rarely flagged as harmful.
conclusion: The findings reveal previously undetected vulnerabilities in aligned LLMs, and the framework can be used to proactively strengthen model safety.

title: PocketAgents: A Manifest-Driven Library Of Autonomous Defense Agents
authors: Sidnei Barbieri, \'agney Lopes Roth Ferraz, Louren\c{c}o Alves Pereira J\'unior
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Connecting large language models (LLMs) to defensive enforcement requires more than asking a model whether an attack is happening. A defender must decide which model outputs may change the system state, which outputs must be rejected, and how failures should be recorded. We present PocketAgents, a manifest-driven library of autonomous defense agents. Each agent is installed as three data files: a manifest, a prompt, and a runtime context. The shared runtime gives the agent bounded telemetry access and accepts only typed reports whose requested action appears in the manifest. We implemented PocketAgents on top of a cyber arena (Perry), a cyber-deception testbed, and evaluated two agents, Command and Control and Exfiltration, in 18 closed-loop trials of a DarkSide-inspired attack on a small enterprise topology. Thirteen trials produced validated network-block actions and contained the attack; four failed schema validation; one produced a valid no-action decision. The experiments show that a typed boundary makes LLM-driven defense measurable, extensible, and attributable.
tldr: PocketAgents is a manifest-driven library for autonomous defense agents using LLMs, evaluated in a cyber-security testbed.
motivation: To address the challenge of making LLM-driven defensive actions measurable, extensible, and attributable in cyber-security contexts.
method: The authors implement a library where each agent is defined by three data files (manifest, prompt, runtime context) and a shared runtime that enforces typed reports and bounded telemetry access. They evaluate two agents in a cyber arena against a simulated DarkSide attack.
result: In 18 trials, 13 produced validated network-block actions containing the attack, 4 failed schema validation, and 1 produced a valid no-action decision.
conclusion: The typed boundary approach makes LLM-driven defense more reliable and auditable, but the paper focuses on cyber-security, not quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: FuzzingBrain V2: A Multi-Agent Llm System For Automated Vulnerability Discovery And Reproduction
authors: Ze Sheng, Zhicheng Chen, Qingxiao Xu, Kewen Zhu, Jeff Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software vulnerabilities pose critical security threats, with nearly 50,000 CVEs reported in 2025. While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for automated vulnerability detection, three key challenges remain. First, LLM-generated vulnerability reports suffer from high false positive rates and lack reproducible verification. Second, existing LLM-based approaches use suboptimal granularities for vulnerability localization: function-level analysis overlooks bugs when context becomes extensive, while line-level analysis lacks sufficient context. Third, existing approaches have difficulty reasoning about vulnerabilities with complex cross-function dependencies and triggering conditions. We present FuzzingBrain V2, a multi-agent system that addresses these gaps through four key contributions: (1) fully automated vulnerability analysis built on Google's OSS-Fuzz, ensuring all reported vulnerabilities are fuzzer-reproducible; (2) Suspicious Point, a novel control-flow-based abstraction for precise vulnerability localization at the optimal granularity; (3) logic-driven hierarchical function analysis with dual-layer fuzzing enhancing function coverage under resource constraints; (4) MCP-based static and dynamic analysis tools with context engineering enhancing complex vulnerability reasoning. On the AIxCC 2025 Final Competition C/C++ dataset, FuzzingBrain V2 achieved 90% detection rate (36 of 40 vulnerabilities). In real-world deployment, FuzzingBrain V2 discovered 29 zero-day vulnerabilities across 12 open-source projects, all confirmed and fixed by maintainers, with 2 assigned CVE IDs.
tldr: FuzzingBrain V2 is a multi-agent LLM system for automated vulnerability discovery and reproduction in software, with no connection to quantum computing or information thermodynamics.
motivation: Software vulnerabilities pose critical security threats, and existing LLM-based approaches suffer from high false positive rates and lack reproducible verification.
method: The system uses a multi-agent LLM architecture with suspicious point abstraction, logic-driven hierarchical function analysis, dual-layer fuzzing, and MCP-based static/dynamic analysis tools.
result: Achieved 90% detection rate on AIxCC 2025 dataset and discovered 29 zero-day vulnerabilities in real-world open-source projects.
conclusion: The approach demonstrates effective automated vulnerability discovery, but the paper is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information and thermodynamics.

title: A Large Language Model Approach To Generating Bypass Rules For Malware Evasion In Analysis Sandbox
authors: Zhiyong Sui, Lamine Noureddine, Mst Eshita Khatun, Sideeq Bello, Justin Woodring, Aisha Ali-Gombe
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sandbox evasion remains a critical challenge for automated malware analysis, as modern malware employs environment checks to detect analysis platforms and suppress malicious behavior. Existing approaches rely on manually crafted bypass rules that require deep reverse engineering of each evasion mechanism -an approach that cannot scale against rapidly evolving evasion techniques. In this paper, we leverage large language models (LLMs) to automatically generate YARA rules that bypass evasion checks in sandbox environments. We propose ABLE, which analyzes execution traces from malware terminated due to potentially evasive behavior and employs multiple reasoning strategies to generate targeted bypass rules. To address syntactic errors and improve the efficacy of the bypass rules in the LLM outputs, we introduce an auto-sanitization pipeline and feedback-driven iterative refinement. We evaluate ABLE on 334 real-world malware samples across four open-weight LLMs. ABLE achieves a 79% bypass success rate, with iterative refinement contributing 29.5% of successful cases. Compared to existing analysis platforms, ABLE identifies 47% more malware family classifications and exposes previously hidden behaviors.
tldr: This paper uses LLMs to generate YARA rules for bypassing sandbox evasion checks in malware analysis, which is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum computing, condensed matter physics, or machine learning.
motivation: Existing sandbox evasion bypass rules require manual reverse engineering and cannot scale against rapidly evolving malware techniques.
method: The authors propose ABLE, which analyzes execution traces from malware and uses LLMs with multiple reasoning strategies, auto-sanitization, and iterative refinement to generate YARA rules.
result: ABLE achieves a 79% bypass success rate on 334 real-world malware samples, with iterative refinement contributing 29.5% of successful cases.
conclusion: The approach improves malware family classification and reveals hidden behaviors, but the paper focuses on cybersecurity, not the user's areas of interest.

title: Quality-Assured Fuzz Harness Generation Via The Four Principles Framework
authors: Ze Sheng, Dmitrijs Trizna, Luigino Camastra, Zhicheng Chen, Qingxiao Xu, Jeff Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21824v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fuzz testing is the dominant technique for finding memory-safety vulnerabilities in C/C++ software, yet its effectiveness hinges on the quality of fuzz harnesses -- the programs that bridge fuzzers and library APIs. A growing body of tools now automate harness generation, but none systematically ensures the correctness of produced harnesses: logic errors, API misuse, and lifecycle violations go undetected at the source level. As LLM-driven generation scales harness creation, uncontrolled quality turns scale into a liability. We present QuartetFuzz, an autonomous harness-generation system that systematically improves correctness throughout the generation process. At its core is the Four Principles framework -- Logic Correctness (P1), API Protocol Compliance (P2), Security Boundary Respect (P3), and Entry Point Adequacy (P4) -- the first source-level definition of harness correctness with mathematical specifications and implementable checks. We operationalize these principles in an autonomous LLM agent that produces harnesses satisfying P1-P4 through a generate-check-fix loop before any fuzzing begins. Deployed on 23 open-source projects spanning C/C++, Java, and JavaScript, the system submits 42 bug reports, of which 29 are fixed or confirmed upstream (including 3 CVEs) and only 2 are rejected (4.8% FP rate). During generation, the built-in P1/P2 checks automatically intercepted 58 harness-induced crashes that would otherwise have been false positives. Applied as a quality auditor to 586 existing production harnesses across 70 projects, the system identifies 53 violations (45 confirmed, 35 fixed). We release a dataset of 100 labeled harnesses for reproducible evaluation. Code and dataset are available at [URL].
tldr: This paper presents QuartetFuzz, an LLM-based system for generating correct fuzz harnesses using a Four Principles framework, applied to C/C++, Java, and JavaScript projects.
motivation: Automated fuzz harness generation often produces incorrect harnesses with logic errors and API misuse, leading to false positives and wasted effort.
method: The authors define four principles (Logic Correctness, API Protocol Compliance, Security Boundary Respect, Entry Point Adequacy) and implement them in an LLM agent that iteratively generates, checks, and fixes harnesses before fuzzing.
result: The system found 42 bugs in 23 projects, with 29 confirmed/fixed (including 3 CVEs) and only 2 rejected (4.8% false positive rate). It also audited 586 existing harnesses, identifying 53 violations.
conclusion: The Four Principles framework and automated loop improve harness correctness, reducing false positives and enabling scalable LLM-driven fuzz testing.

title: Spider: Two Server Functionality For The Cost Of Zero
authors: Ofir Dvir, Kali Hale, Javin Zipkin, Divyakant Agrawal, Dahlia Malkhi
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce baseSPIDER and SPIDER, private information retrieval (PIR) schemes that embody two technical advancements. The baseSPIDER protocol operates with a single server and a stateful client that performs pre-processing and stores hints for future queries. In this setting, baseSPIDER introduces a new approach that matches the asymptotically optimal communication complexity of state-of-the-art schemes while improving constant factors--an advantage that is particularly significant for databases with large entries. In addition, baseSPIDER offers a conceptually simpler design relative to prior protocols. SPIDER operates over a default database interface and requires no cooperation from the server at any stage. To our knowledge, SPIDER is the first single-server PIR construction of this design, achieving privacy without specialized APIs, auxiliary server state, or protocol-specific interaction beyond conventional indexed access. SPIDER is built via a simple transformation of baseSPIDER to the default server setting, eliminating deployment barriers and enabling immediate applicability to existing systems. This transformation can be applied more broadly to three recent PIR solutions, adapting them for use in the default-server paradigm and yielding solutions of independent interest. SPIDER compares to the resulting modified solutions by exhibiting a simpler design while incurring higher client computational work.
tldr: This paper presents SPIDER, a single-server private information retrieval scheme that achieves privacy without specialized server APIs, focusing on communication complexity and deployment simplicity.
motivation: To reduce deployment barriers for private information retrieval by eliminating the need for server-side modifications or specialized protocols.
method: The authors introduce baseSPIDER, a stateful single-server PIR with pre-processing, and transform it into SPIDER, which operates over a default database interface without server cooperation.
result: SPIDER matches asymptotic optimal communication complexity with improved constant factors and offers a simpler design compared to prior schemes.
conclusion: SPIDER enables immediate applicability to existing systems, and the transformation technique can be applied to other PIR solutions.

title: CCLab: Adversarial Testing Of Learning- And Non-Learning-Based Congestion Controllers
authors: Zhi Chen, Shehab Sarar Ahmed, Chenkai Wang, Brighten Godfrey, Gang Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21915v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Congestion controllers (CCs) are critical to network performance, and yet their robustness under adverse conditions remains insufficiently understood. While recent learning-based CCs have demonstrated strong performance in controlled environments, it is unclear how they compare to traditional CCs when controllers' input signals are corrupted or when environmental conditions become systematically challenging. In this paper, we introduce CCLab, an adversarial testing framework for systematically evaluating the robustness of both learning-based and non-learning-based CCs. CCLab includes a reinforcement learning (RL)-based adversarial agent that operates in a closed loop with the congestion control policy, generating bounded perturbations either on input signals (feature-level) or on external network conditions (environment-level), while preserving realism through explicit constraints. Using this framework, we compare learning-based CCs with non-learning-based CCs under both feature-level and environment-level adversarial conditions. While both types of CCs suffer from performance degradation under adversarial testing, we find that learning-based CCs, in general, are more robust than traditional human-designed algorithms. Finally, we show that our adversarial traces can be used to train more robust CCs that outperform existing learning-based CCs under both challenging and normal conditions.
tldr: This paper presents CCLab, an adversarial testing framework for congestion controllers, but is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The robustness of congestion controllers under adversarial conditions is not well understood, especially for learning-based versus traditional algorithms.
method: The authors develop CCLab, which uses a reinforcement learning-based adversarial agent to generate bounded perturbations on input signals or network conditions, and evaluate both learning-based and non-learning-based congestion controllers.
result: Both types of controllers suffer performance degradation under adversarial testing, but learning-based controllers are generally more robust than traditional ones.
conclusion: Adversarial traces can be used to train more robust congestion controllers that outperform existing ones under both challenging and normal conditions.

title: Single-Item Auctions With A Monopolist Intermediary
authors: Jingyi Liu, Aviad Rubinstein, Ertem Nusret Tas, S. Matthew Weinberg, Qianfan Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.21934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical optimal auction theory assumes that bids reach the seller directly. We study how this picture changes when a revenue-maximizing intermediary controls access to the seller's auction. Motivated by blockchain auctions, online platforms, and other intermediated markets, we consider a single-item auction with independent private values and a monopolist intermediary who can decide which bidder messages are forwarded to the seller. We establish approximation guarantees and impossibility results across three timing models: seller-first, intermediary-first, and simultaneous. In the seller-first model, arbitrary deterministic seller mechanisms collapse to posted-price mechanisms, and the intermediary's best response is a shifted Myerson auction. This yields a sharp separation: for regular distributions, the seller's revenue can be arbitrarily small relative to the no-intermediary optimum, while for [MATH]-strongly regular distributions, posted prices recover a constant fraction of the optimum with a tight dependence on [MATH]. We further show that timing matters: neither Stackelberg order uniformly dominates, and simultaneous play can leave both parties unboundedly worse off than in either sequential model.
tldr: This paper studies optimal auction design with a revenue-maximizing intermediary, focusing on blockchain and online platform contexts.
motivation: To understand how a monopolist intermediary affects seller revenue in single-item auctions, motivated by blockchain and online platforms.
method: The authors analyze three timing models (seller-first, intermediary-first, simultaneous) using game theory and mechanism design.
result: They show that seller-first collapses to posted-price mechanisms, and for regular distributions seller revenue can be arbitrarily low; for strongly regular distributions, posted prices achieve constant approximation.
conclusion: Timing matters significantly, and simultaneous play can be much worse for both parties than sequential models.

title: Blind Spots In The Guard: How Domain-Camouflaged Injection Attacks Evade Detection In Multi-Agent Llm Systems
authors: Aaditya Pai
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22001v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Injection detectors deployed to protect LLM agents are calibrated on static, template-based payloads that announce themselves as override directives. We identify a systematic blind spot: when payloads are generated to mimic the domain vocabulary and authority structures of the target document, what we call domain camouflaged injection, standard detectors fail to flag them, with detection rates dropping from 93.8% to 9.7% on Llama 3.1 8B and from 100% to 55.6% on Gemini 2.0 Flash. We formalize this as the Camouflage Detection Gap (CDG), the difference in injection detection rate between static and camouflaged payloads. Across 45 tasks spanning three domains and two model families, CDG is large and statistically significant (chi^2 = 38.03, p < 0.001 for Llama; chi^2 = 17.05, p < 0.001 for Gemini), with zero reverse discordant pairs in either case. We additionally evaluate Llama Guard 3, a production safety classifier, which detects zero camouflage payloads (IDRcamouflage = 0.000), confirming that the blind spot extends beyond few-shot detectors to dedicated safety classifiers. We further show that multi-agent debate architectures amplify static injection attacks by up to 9.9x on smaller models, while stronger models show collective resistance. Targeted detector augmentation provides only partial remediation (10.2% improvement on Llama, 78.7% on Gemini), suggesting the vulnerability is architectural rather than incidental for weaker models. Our framework, task bank, and payload generator are released publicly.
tldr: This paper identifies a blind spot in LLM injection detectors where domain-camouflaged payloads evade detection, and evaluates multi-agent debate architectures.
motivation: Current injection detectors are calibrated on static payloads and fail against payloads that mimic domain vocabulary and authority structures.
method: The authors formalize the Camouflage Detection Gap (CDG) and evaluate detection rates on Llama 3.1 8B, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and Llama Guard 3 across 45 tasks in three domains.
result: Detection rates drop from 93.8% to 9.7% on Llama and 100% to 55.6% on Gemini; Llama Guard 3 detects zero camouflage payloads. Multi-agent debate amplifies static injection attacks on smaller models.
conclusion: The vulnerability is architectural for weaker models; targeted detector augmentation provides partial remediation. The framework and payload generator are released publicly.

title: Parser-Free Querying Of Security Logs
authors: Evan Luo, Julien Piet, David Wagner
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security analysts routinely query system logs to detect threats and investigate incidents, but each log source uses its own semi-structured format: logs are cheap to produce, but expensive to use. The standard approach, building per-source parsers to normalize logs into structured schemas, is powerful but requires continuous engineering effort for each new format. Querying raw logs directly with tools like grep avoids this cost, but requires analysts to know each source's message variants and cannot express the multi-line temporal queries that security investigations demand. We present Sieve, a system that generates executable query code from natural-language security questions by grounding a large language model with lightweight, automatically extracted log-format context, requiring only one LLM call per query followed by deterministic execution. Evaluating 133 security queries across 5 log types, we find that Sieve achieves over a 3x reduction in error rate on complex temporal and cross-event queries compared to manual analyst scripting, with the largest gains on the multi-line correlation tasks most critical to active investigations. Our results and benchmark provide evidence that LLM-generated code can bridge the gap between the expressiveness of structured log querying and the immediacy of working directly with raw files.
tldr: Sieve is a system that uses LLMs to generate executable queries from natural language for security log analysis, bypassing the need for per-source parsers.
motivation: Security log analysis is hindered by diverse semi-structured formats requiring custom parsers; existing tools like grep lack expressiveness for complex temporal queries.
method: Sieve combines a single LLM call with automatically extracted log-format context to generate executable query code, then runs it deterministically.
result: On 133 security queries across 5 log types, Sieve reduces error rate by over 3x compared to manual scripting, especially for multi-line correlation tasks.
conclusion: LLM-generated code can bridge the gap between structured querying and raw log analysis, reducing engineering effort while maintaining expressiveness.

title: Radar: Defending Rag Dynamically Against Retrieval Corruption
authors: Ziyuan Chen, Yueming Lyu, Yi Liu, Weixiang Han, Jing Dong, Caifeng Shan, Tieniu Tan
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22041v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While RAG systems are increasingly deployed in dynamic web search, temporal volatility amplifies their vulnerability to adversarial attacks. Existing static-oriented defenses struggle to handle evolving threats and incur prohibitive storage costs in dynamic settings. We propose RADAR, a framework that models reliable context selection as a graph-based energy minimization problem, solved exactly via Max-Flow Min-Cut. By incorporating a Bayesian memory node, RADAR recursively updates a belief state instead of archiving raw historical documents, effectively balancing stability against attacks with adaptability to genuine knowledge shifts. Experiments on a novel dynamic dataset show that RADAR achieves superior robustness and response quality with minimal storage overhead compared to the baselines.
tldr: RADAR is a defense framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems against adversarial retrieval corruption, using graph-based energy minimization and Bayesian memory.
motivation: RAG systems in dynamic web search are vulnerable to evolving adversarial attacks, and existing static defenses are costly and ineffective.
method: Models reliable context selection as a graph-based energy minimization problem solved via Max-Flow Min-Cut, with a Bayesian memory node for recursive belief updates.
result: RADAR achieves superior robustness and response quality with minimal storage overhead on a novel dynamic dataset.
conclusion: The framework offers a scalable defense for dynamic RAG systems, balancing stability and adaptability.

title: Human Vulnerability Assessment In Cybersecurity: A Systematic Literature Review Of Methods, Models, And Instruments
authors: Dimitra Papatsaroucha, Stavroula Psaroudaki, Eleftheria Vassilaki, Konstantina Pityanou, Evangelos K. Markakis
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In cybersecurity, vulnerability assessment has typically focused on identifying and measuring vulnerabilities within digital assets and technical infrastructures. However, there is growing recognition that this approach alone is inadequate without a structured examination of the human factor, which is becoming more frequently targeted and manipulated by cyber adversaries. Human vulnerabilities extend beyond individual susceptibility to cyber threats, encompassing a wide array of psychological, cognitive, behavioral, social, and contextual factors that can, whether unintentionally or intentionally, jeopardize the security and integrity of systems and data. Despite this recognition, human vulnerability assessment remains fragmented, often addressed from a static rather than a dynamic perspective, and with limited focus on the ways it propagates across individuals and systems; a growing body of literature has explored specific facets of the issue, including one-time assessments of security behavior, user awareness, and, to a degree, intentional insider threats and their detection. This research offers a systematic literature review (SLR) of Human Vulnerability Assessment (HVA) in cybersecurity, including methods, models, and instruments proposed for the conceptual or practical assessment of human vulnerabilities across various dimensions. Following the PRISMA framework, this review gathers relevant studies published from 2017 to 2025, aiming to investigate whether any assessment methods, models, or instruments exist that address the entire spectrum of human vulnerabilities dynamically. The findings highlight gaps and limitations in current proposed solutions and identify areas for further investigation regarding holistic assessment that simultaneously and dynamically considers the entire spectrum of both the unintentional and intentional dimensions of human vulnerability.
tldr: This paper is a systematic literature review on human vulnerability assessment in cybersecurity, focusing on psychological, cognitive, and social factors, with no connection to quantum computing or the user's research interests.
motivation: The research was conducted to address the fragmented and static nature of human vulnerability assessment in cybersecurity, recognizing the growing importance of the human factor.
method: The authors performed a systematic literature review following the PRISMA framework, gathering studies from 2017 to 2025 on methods, models, and instruments for human vulnerability assessment.
result: The review identified gaps and limitations in current approaches, particularly the lack of holistic and dynamic assessment covering both unintentional and intentional human vulnerabilities.
conclusion: The findings highlight the need for further research into comprehensive, dynamic assessment methods that consider the full spectrum of human vulnerabilities.

title: Benchmarking Autonomous Agents Against Temporal, Spatial, And Semantic Evasions
authors: Jianan Ma, Xiaohu Du, Ruixiao Lin, Yaoxiang Bian, Jialuo Chen, Jingyi Wang, Xiaofang Yang, Shiwen Cui, Changhua Meng, Xinhao Deng, Zhen Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As autonomous agents (e.g., OpenClaw) increasingly operate with deep system-level privileges to execute complex tasks, they introduce severe, unmitigated security risks. Current vulnerability analyses overwhelmingly focus on single-turn, stateless behaviors, overlooking the expanded attack surface inherent in stateful, multi-turn interactions and dynamic tool invocations. In this paper, we propose a novel, multi-dimensional evasion framework targeting LLM-based agent systems. We introduce three stealthy attack vectors: (1) Temporal evasion, which fragments malicious payloads across sequential interaction turns; (2) Spatial evasion, which conceals payloads within complex external artifacts that evade standard LLM parsing mechanisms; and (3) Semantic evasion, which obscures malicious intents beneath benign contextual noise. To systematically quantify these threats, we construct A3S-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark comprising 2,254 real-world agent execution trajectories. Evaluating a standard agent framework separately integrated with 10 mainstream LLM backbones against 20 practical threat scenarios, we demonstrate that our evasion framework elevates the average risk trigger rate from a 28.3\% baseline to 52.6\%. These findings reveal systemic, architecture-level vulnerabilities in current autonomous agent systems that existing defenses fail to address, highlighting an urgent need for defense mechanisms tailored to the unique threats.
tldr: This paper proposes a multi-dimensional evasion framework for LLM-based autonomous agents, introducing temporal, spatial, and semantic attack vectors, and benchmarks them on a new dataset.
motivation: To address security vulnerabilities in stateful, multi-turn autonomous agent systems that are overlooked by current single-turn, stateless vulnerability analyses.
method: The authors design three stealthy attack vectors (temporal, spatial, semantic evasion) and construct A3S-Bench, a benchmark of 2,254 real-world agent trajectories, evaluating 10 LLM backbones against 20 threat scenarios.
result: The evasion framework increases the average risk trigger rate from 28.3% to 52.6%, revealing systemic vulnerabilities in current autonomous agent systems.
conclusion: Existing defenses are insufficient against these new attack vectors, highlighting the need for tailored defense mechanisms for autonomous agents.

title: Pact: Reducing Alert Fatigue In Low-Prevalence Soc Streams With Triggered Active Learning
authors: Samuel Ndichu, Tao Ban, Seiichi Ozawa, Takeshi Takahashi, Daisuke Inoue
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security operations centers face persistent alert fatigue: in low-prevalence streams, even low false-positive rates generate substantial investigation load, while aggregate F1 scores obscure analyst burden. We introduce PACT, a Pareto-aware controller for triggered active learning, which wraps an already-deployed frozen XGBoost-Focal screener with an adaptive windowing score-shift trigger and a hybrid acquisition rule combining threshold-relative uncertainty with high-score sampling. On two public low-prevalence benchmarks, AIT-ADS (AIT Alert Data Set), and BOTSv1 (Boss of the SOC version 1), PACT attains the lowest benign-normalized false-positive (FP) burden among the adaptive methods tested. It reduces burden by 43% and 21%, respectively, relative to a frozen baseline, while using 3.8x and 5.2x fewer analyst queries than periodic uniform-random updating. A matched-trigger ablation controls trigger timing and shows that acquisition contributes beyond timing alone, at the cost of approximately ten percentage points of positive-window recall under free-running triggers. A frozen threshold-only baseline pushes FP lower still but collapses BOTSv1 recall by 55 percentage points. Under the evaluated workload assumptions, pure FP minimization trades unacceptable recall for that lower burden.
tldr: PACT is a triggered active learning method to reduce alert fatigue in security operations centers, using a Pareto-aware controller to minimize false positives while maintaining recall.
motivation: Security operations centers suffer from alert fatigue due to low-prevalence streams where even low false-positive rates cause high investigation load, and aggregate F1 scores do not capture analyst burden.
method: PACT wraps a frozen XGBoost-Focal screener with an adaptive windowing score-shift trigger and a hybrid acquisition rule combining threshold-relative uncertainty with high-score sampling.
result: On AIT-ADS and BOTSv1 benchmarks, PACT reduces benign-normalized false-positive burden by 43% and 21% relative to a frozen baseline, using 3.8x and 5.2x fewer analyst queries than periodic uniform-random updating.
conclusion: PACT effectively reduces alert fatigue with minimal analyst queries, but pure false-positive minimization can lead to unacceptable recall loss, highlighting the need for balanced approaches.

title: A First Measurement Study On Authentication Security In Real-World Remote Mcp Servers
authors: Huijun Zhou, Xiaohan Zhang, Haozhe Zhang, Haoyang Zhang, Mi Zhang, Min Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is emerging as a common interface connecting large language models (LLMs) with external services. Remote deployments are becoming increasingly important as agents connect to user-linked online services, such as social, productivity, and financial services. In such deployments, the authentication boundary between MCP clients and remote servers becomes security-critical, yet remains underexplored. We present the first measurement study of authentication security in real-world remote MCP servers. We identify 7,973 live remote MCP servers, finding that 40.55% expose tools without authentication. Among authenticated servers, OAuth is the dominant authorization mechanism for reaching remote services, and OAuth deployments in the MCP ecosystem commonly exhibit three characteristics: open client environments, dynamic client registration, and delegated authorization. These characteristics distinguish MCP deployments from traditional OAuth and introduce new attack surfaces. Guided by this observation, we derive a taxonomy of authentication flaws comprising three MCP-specific categories and conventional OAuth misconfigurations, for a total of four categories and nine concrete flaw types. To evaluate these flaws at scale, we implement a semi-automated detection framework that combines passive traffic inspection with active dynamic probing. Applying it to 119 testable real-world OAuth-enabled MCP servers, we find that each server exhibits at least one flaw, with a total of 325 flaws identified, among which dynamic client registration flaws affect 96.6% of tested servers. Many of these flaws can lead to sensitive information leakage and account takeover. Through responsible disclosure, we obtained 9 CVE IDs. Our findings expose pervasive authentication weaknesses in the MCP ecosystem and underscore the urgent need for hardened OAuth-based remote deployments.
tldr: This paper measures authentication security in real-world remote MCP servers, finding widespread flaws and vulnerabilities.
motivation: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is emerging for LLM-external service connections, but authentication security in remote deployments is underexplored.
method: The authors identified 7,973 live remote MCP servers, analyzed OAuth deployments, and built a semi-automated detection framework combining passive traffic inspection and active probing.
result: 40.55% of servers expose tools without authentication; among OAuth-enabled servers, 96.6% have dynamic client registration flaws, with 325 total flaws across 119 tested servers.
conclusion: The MCP ecosystem has pervasive authentication weaknesses, requiring hardened OAuth deployments to prevent information leakage and account takeover.

title: TimeGuard: Channel-wise Pool Training For Backdoor Defense In Time Series Forecasting
authors: Quang Duc Nguyen, Siyuan Liang, Yiming Li, Fushuo Huo, Dacheng Tao
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time Series Forecasting (TSF) plays a critical role across many domains, yet it is vulnerable to backdoor attacks. However, backdoor defenses tailored to TSF remain underexplored, due to data entanglement and task-formulation shift challenges. To fill this gap, we conduct a systematic evaluation of thirteen representative backdoor defenses across the TSF life cycle and analyze their failure modes. Our results reveal two fundamental issues: (1) data entanglement induces channel-level signal dilution, rendering sample-filtering and trigger-synthesis defenses ineffective at localizing backdoors; and (2) task-formulation shift leads to training-loss degeneration, causing poisoned and clean windows to become indistinguishable at training stages. Based on these findings, we propose a training-time backdoor defense for TSF, termed TimeGuard. Our method adopts channel-wise pool training as the core paradigm and initializes a high-confidence pool using time-aware criteria to mitigate signal dilution. Moreover, we introduce distance-regularized loss selection to progressively expand the reliable pool during training and ease loss degeneration. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets, forecasting architectures, and TSF backdoor attacks demonstrate that TimeGuard substantially improves robustness, boosting [MATH] by [MATH] over the leading baseline, while preserving clean performance within 5% [MATH].
tldr: This paper proposes a backdoor defense method for time series forecasting, which is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information and thermodynamics.
motivation: Time series forecasting is vulnerable to backdoor attacks, but existing defenses are ineffective due to data entanglement and task-formulation shift.
method: The authors propose TimeGuard, which uses channel-wise pool training with time-aware criteria and distance-regularized loss selection to mitigate backdoor attacks.
result: TimeGuard improves robustness against backdoor attacks while preserving clean performance within 5% of the original.
conclusion: The method provides a new defense paradigm for time series forecasting, but its relevance to quantum computing or information thermodynamics is negligible.

title: A Constant-Time Implementation Methodology For Activation Functions On Microcontrollers
authors: Andrii Tyvodar, Andreas Rechberger, Dirmanto Jap, Shivam Bhasin, Bernhard Jungk, Jakub Breier, Xiaolu Hou
abstract: ArXiv:2605.22441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embedded neural-network inference can leak information through timing side channels, including leakage caused by the evaluation of activation functions. This work proposes a constant-time implementation methodology for activation functions on embedded microcontrollers and validates it on ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, GELU, and Swish on an ARM Cortex-M4 platform. The proposed methodology combines branchless selection, fixed-cost Pad\'e-based approximation, dummy arithmetic where needed, and cycle alignment to obtain timing-regular activation-function implementations. As motivation, we also evaluate a desynchronization-based countermeasure and show that it remains vulnerable to a template-based timing attack. Experimental results show that the resulting protected implementations achieve identical cycle counts for all tested inputs, including (88) cycles in the three-function setting and (108) cycles in the five-function setting. At the same time, the numerical-error analysis indicates that the approximated nonlinear functions retain high accuracy. These results suggest that the proposed methodology provides a practical basis for constructing side-channel-resistant activation functions in embedded inference.
tldr: This paper presents a constant-time implementation methodology for activation functions on microcontrollers to prevent timing side-channel attacks.
motivation: Embedded neural-network inference can leak information through timing side channels, particularly from activation function evaluation. Existing countermeasures like desynchronization remain vulnerable.
method: The methodology combines branchless selection, fixed-cost Padé-based approximation, dummy arithmetic, and cycle alignment to achieve timing-regular implementations of ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, GELU, and Swish on ARM Cortex-M4.
result: Protected implementations achieve identical cycle counts for all tested inputs (88 cycles for three functions, 108 for five) while maintaining high numerical accuracy.
conclusion: The proposed methodology provides a practical basis for constructing side-channel-resistant activation functions in embedded inference, with potential for extension to other functions and platforms.
